<meta>continues from previous page</meta>They sold land and houses for Cheng to live in. The other brothers were enraged that they were currying favor, so they went to their door to harass and humiliate them. Cheng had long been living among bandits and had become accustomed to violence. Upon hearing this, he was furious and said, "I have returned, yet no one is willing to provide a single room. Fortunately, my third younger brother remembers our kinship, yet you reproach him for it. Are you trying to drive me away?" He threw stones at Xiao. Xiao, Ren, and Yi each took up a staff and drove them out. They took Zhong and Xin and beat them both countless times. Cheng did not wait for them to sue; he sued them before the magistrate first. The magistrate then sent someone to summon Youyu. Youyu, having no choice, came. When asked, they all hung their heads in shame and said nothing, only weeping. When the magistrate pressed them for an answer, they only asked for an official judgment. The magistrate then ruled that Xiao and the others must each contribute a portion of their land and property to Cheng, such that the assets would be divided into seven equal shares. From then on, Ren, Yi, and Cheng became even more affectionate and respectful toward one another. During a conversation, they suddenly touched upon the matter of their mother’s burial and all began to weep. Cheng said, "To be so unfilial as this is like a beast." He then intended to exhume the grave and rebury her. Ren and Yi ran to inform Youyu. Youyu hurried home to remonstrate and stop them, but Cheng would not listen and set a date for the act.

<summary>Cheng, having returned from his time with bandits, defends his brothers Ren and Yi against the harassment of the other siblings. The magistrate orders a redistribution of the family property, and the brothers reconcile, leading to a plan to rebury their mother with greater respect.</summary>
<keywords>Cheng, Ren, Yi, Youyu, magistrate, family conflict, filial piety, burial</keywords>
